diagram is a method of identifying exploring and  organizing the possible factors that contribute to
a particular problem or effect the object of the  fishbone diagram is to identify the actual cause
of a problem not just the symptoms of that  problem the fishbone diagram is also known
as the cause and effect diagram or the ishakawa  diagram taking the name of its creator k ishakawa
a business analyst might use a fishbone diagram  to perform a root cause analysis perform a cause
and effect analysis facilitate quality improvement  efforts identify process Improvement opportunities
anticipate and prevent potential risks and issues  or to specify an effective solution or corrective
action to an issue now let's look at the main  components of ishikawa's fishbone diagram the
first component of the diagram is the problem  this is a high Lev description of the issue
or effect that needs to be understood it's the  focus of the diagram and serves as the starting
point to explore all of the potential causes  that might be contributing to it the problem
in a fishbone diagram usually originates from  a well formed problem statement this statement
serves as the foundation of your entire analysis  clearly outlining the issue at hand the problem
is commonly Illustrated as a large fish head at  the far right of the diagram that's labeled with
the effect of that problem it's essentially a  visual reminder of the problem you're trying to
understand the problem can also be represented by  any other shape that's a appropriate for the style
of the fishbone diagram what's important is that  the problem is the largest item on the diagram and
that there's only one problem to focus on the next  fishbone diagram component is the cause categories
these are the main categories representing the  general causes of the problem the categories of
the causes may be derived using various methods  including 8 m 8ps or 4 s's the 8 M's categories
are applicable in manufacturing and production  environments where the focus is on the production
process process the categories include Manpower  machines materials methods management measurement
maintenance and mother nature Manpower refers  to the people involved in the process machines
are the equipment and tools used in the process  materials identify the raw materials components
and supplies within the related process  methods are the procedures and processes
followed in the organization management considers  the leadership and decision-making aspects of the
related Process Measurement refers to the metrics  and data used to assess performance maintenance
is the upkeep repair and preventive maintenance  activities performed on equipment and machinery
and mother nature looks at the impact of the  environment on the process such as temperature
humidity lighting and other Natural Factors now  the eight PS method is particularly useful in
product marketing Industries where service and  customer experience play significant roles in
addressing issues such as in service Industries  retail hospitality and education the categories
in the AP PS method include product place people  process promotion productivity price and physical
evidence product refers to the actual goods or  services offered by the company Place involves the
distribution and availability of the product or  service people encompasses the Personnel involved
in delivering the product or service process  refers to the procedures and methods used to
deliver the product or service promotion involves  the marketing and communication strategies used
to promote the product or service productivity  represents the efficiency and effectiveness of
the production process price relates to the cost  of the product or service pricing strategies
consider factors such as production cost market  demand and competitor pricing physical evidence
also known as packaging refers to the tangible  elements or representations that customer use
to evaluate the service one note about the 8 M's  and 8ps methods is that some of the categories
can be removed from the fish phone diagram  if they're not applicable then there's the
four s's this approach is used in Industries  where external factors and relationships play
a significant role for example Supply Chain  management or retail the four ess's categories
include surroundings suppliers systems and skills  surroundings involve the external environmental
factors of the organization suppliers refer  to the external entities providing materials
or services to the organization systems Define  the larger Network work in which the process of
Interest operates skills are the competencies of  individuals involved in the process of Interest
the last fishbone diagram component outlines the  sub causes these represent the potential issues
that are likely to be contributing to the problem  being investigated in the cause and effect or root
cause analysis sub causes of the fishbone diagram  are grouped into the cause categories to visually
represent the relationships to one another  and their respective categories subclauses are
represented at three levels a primary cause is a  specific issue that contributes to a problem these
are the biggest branches on the fishbone diagram  they're indicated by a line that directly touches
the backbone of the fishbone diagram to the cause  category they're labeled with general terms that
describe the underlying factors contributing to  the problem once the primary cause is identified
ask if the primary cause fully explains the  problem if the proper calls alone provides
a clear and sufficient explanation of the issue  exploring second AR causes might not be necessary
but if you still have lingering doubts secondary  causes can help address these uncertainties here
you'll generally focus on why and how type of  questions such as why is this the cause this
question helps you drill down to the underlying  reason for the primary cause for example if the
primary cause is poor customer service ask why  was the customer service poor or how was this
CA contributing to the problem this question  clarifies how the secondary cost specifically
connect the primary cause and ultimately the  main problem now a secondary CA within the
fishbone diagram provides detail that explains  how the primary cause contributes to the problem
being investigated it's also directly related to  the primary cause this is Illustrated as smaller
branches stemming from the primary cause Branch  when identifying the secondary cause you may ask
what else as there may be several secondary causes  stemming from one primary cause but be careful not
to make the Fishbone diagram too complex once  the secondary cause has been identified ask if
actionable insights or practical Solutions can be  defined from the results if not you may need to
identify a tertiary cause also ask if more details  are still needed to fully understand the secondary
cause and how it operates if not you don't need to  go any further but if more details are needed this
would be another case to identify the tertiary  cause the tertiary cause of the fishbone diagram
provides insight into to the specific mechanisms  by which the secondary cause contributes to the
problem and why it exists understanding tertiary  causes during a cause and effect analysis can
inform more targeted Solutions but while these  details are more specific they're often indirectly
related to the primary cause because of this the  tertiary branches are considered optional tertiary
causes are represented by the smallest lines  on the fish bond diagram branching out from the
secondary cause now let's look at an example  for each type of sub cause for the Manpower
category for investigating poor customer service  a primary cause identified might be insufficient
Staffing this would directly and immediately cause  poor customer service because there wouldn't be
enough staff members to accommodate the customer  demand which would lead to Extended wait times
here we may still need to ask why is Staffing  insufficient the response to this may be that the
current hiring process is leading to high turnover  from there we may ask for additional details such
as which part of the hiring process is leading  to the high turnover a possible response might
be that inadequate onboarding is leading to high  turnover because we're setting up new team members

steps to create a fishbone diagram for a cause and  effect analysis or a root cause analysis the first
step is to clearly Define the problem this will be  represented as the effect or the fish head in the
diagram if appropriate you can add information  regarding the details of the problem and its
effects next gather the subject matter experts  here the business analyst will need to formulate
a team of individuals who are familiar with the  process functions and problem in question then
you'll create the fishbone diagram template draw  the outline on a large piece of paper whiteboard
or a diagramming tool the template should include  a problem node several cause categories and lines
for sub causes it should resemble the spine and  scales of a fishbone hence the name now you'll
need to determine the cause categories based on  your knowledge of the organization choose the
cause categories method that will most effectively  represent the possible causes of the problem this
might be the 8 M's method the 8ps or the four  s's once selected fill in the cause categories
appropriately now it's time to identify possible  causes here your brain storm with subject matter
experts to determine the possible causes that  may be contributing to the problem that has
been defined here the business analyst can guide  the stakeholders through each cause category by
using prompts and questions this will generate  the various primary causes within each cause
category for example when brainstorming for  the Manpower category you may ask questions
like what skills or knowledge are missing in  the team are there any communication issues
or misunderstandings or is there sufficient  training provided to the employees this is a
creative and open-minded process where all ideas  are welcome then you'll need to further analyze
the causes you can further analyze them to  identify secondary and tertiary causes for
the secondary cause ask for explanations on why  the primary cause contributes to the problem
for the tertiary cause ask questions regarding  the details and breakdown of the related cause
to understand the functions and mechanisms of the  secondary cause at this point the cause and effect
analysis is complete but there's more if you're  using the fishbone diagram to perform a root cause
analysis the next step is to prioritize the causes  due to the volume of potential causes identified
it will be necessary to narrow down the causes to  a few that will be further analyzed to determine
the actual root causes the business analyst can  work with the subject matter expert to identify
the causes that are likely to have the highest  impact on the problem this is often done using
the Paro principle this method uses the 8020 rule  to determine the 20% of causes that are leading to
80% of the effects or results determining the most  impactful causes can be facilitated through multiv
voting here the business analyst will provide the  subject matter experts with the voting or point
system each participant votes on the causes they  believe have the most significant impact on the
problem allocating their votes accordingly now  we're ready to perform the root cause analysis
after the most impactful primary causes have  been identified facilitate root cause analysis
on each using the five yse technique for example  the primary cause of lack of training with the
secondary cause of poor Communications of training  requirements might involve questions like why were
the training requirements poorly communicated  why did the training manager not provide
clear instructions why was the training manager  overloaded with work why was their High turnover

plan after the group agrees on the root cause or  causes discuss solutions to correct the problem or
prevent it from recurring now let's go through  some best practices for creating a fishbone
diagram and performing a root cause analysis  first focus on the causes when brainstorming
causes for the fishbone diagram ensure that the  group focuses on the causes not Solutions at this
this stage it could be tempting to lead into  Solutions during this time but the facilitator
should be prepared to reserve that discussion  for later also identify the fact distinguish
causes as facts that are proven by data or beliefs  that are driven by common knowledge or opinions
any cause categorized as a belief will need to be  investigated and validated following the session
involve cross functional teams gather a diverse  group of stakeholders with different perspectives
and expertise relevant to the problem this ensures  a comprehensive consideration of the various
factors for the root cause analysis prioritize  the causes. performing a root cause analysis on
every potential cost can be time consuming.  Prioritization optimizes the team's time by
ensuring that additional root cost efforts  are only directed towards the most critical
issue use common language write the fishbone  diagram labels and items in clear and concise
language avoid jargon or overly technical terms  to ensure that the diagram is easily understood
by the entire group consistent symbols and colors  should be used to represent specific elements of
the fishbone diagram this helps in creating an  intuitive and easy to understand diagram and
finally Define an action plan for the root cause  analysis a fishbone diagram is useless without a
